summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists. The Act reaches beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Kaduna is one of the twelve states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces that jurisdiction to Zamfara's governor introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, after which by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation.

The state carries two stacked criminal layers, and the secular one is harsher than the federal ceiling. Section 3.1.6 and 8.2.19 of the Home Office note record that Kaduna adopted its own Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' including sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, above the federal 14-year maximum.

The Sharia layer is Kaduna's own promulgated code rather than umbrella coverage. Ostien's annotated volume lists the Sharia Penal Code Law 2002, Law No. 4 of 2002, signed into law and coming into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code). Its annotation records Kaduna as one of only three states whose enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), with no unmarried or married graduation, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment. The Home Office's twelve-state penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived) carries Kaduna's row on the same terms: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat, and same-sex acts between women punishable at the discretion of the qadi.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

No trans-specific incident and no documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Kaduna in these sources, and no court-level study samples the state. The evidence for Kaduna rests on its enacted statutes rather than on reported prosecutions.
tangentialFactors:
Kaduna's secular ceiling sits above the national one. Section 259 of the 2017 Penal Code carries up to 21 years plus a fine for unnatural offences, against the federal 14-year maximum under the SSMPA and the secular provisions described by the Home Office, so a visitor in Kaduna faces a longer nominal term than the same conduct would draw in states without their own penal code.

The state is also an outlier within the Sharia bloc on the text of its capital provision. Ostien's annotation identifies Kaduna as one of only three states whose enacted wording mandates stoning to death for sodomy without the unmarried or married graduation found elsewhere, which places it at the top of the twelve-state range rather than at its midpoint.

Two of the sources sit at different levels of the same architecture: the Home Office table derives its Kaduna row from ILGA material, while Ostien's volume works from the gazetted text itself. They agree on the outcome, and the enactment-level record is the stronger of the two.

Enforcement evidence for the state is thin compared with the statutory evidence. The documented incidents in these sources come from Abuja and Lagos, and the pattern they establish is national rather than Kaduna-specific.

Nigerian citizenship does not shield anyone from the SSMPA, which reaches cohabitation, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and which Human Rights Watch records as having been used by police to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Housing between male and female sections on imprisonment is left to institutional discretion. In the Bobrisky case an October 2024 investigative panel found that placement in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here, so the current exposure for gender expression in Kaduna cannot be stated as settled law.

No prosecution, arrest or Hisbah enforcement action under either Kaduna statute is documented in these sources. The state-level findings rest on enacted text and penalty tables, and no court-level study samples Kaduna.

Whether the stoning penalty recorded in Kaduna's 2002 text has been imposed or carried out is not sourced here.

The 2017 Kaduna Penal Code and the 2002 Sharia Penal Code are described as operating in parallel, but the sources do not explain how the two are applied together in a single case, or whether the Sharia layer is limited to Muslims in practice as the Home Office note indicates.
